name: Carlos Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a crew lead at Halden Electrical, a contractor with about thirty sparkies, and I run a crew of four. Most days we're rewiring old houses, the ones with cloth-covered cable and fuse boxes from before my dad was born, plus small shops and the odd café. I'm in the van by seven, pick up Dani (my apprentice) on the way, and I spend the day half on the tools and half making sure nobody on my crew gets hurt. What I love is finding the fault nobody else could find. What wears me out is the office phoning me five times a day about paperwork.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing this, and how did you get to be the one running the crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nine years, since I was eighteen. I got my master's licence last year, which is why they gave me the crew. I'm good at it because I'm careful and I don't cut corners, and the old guys trust me. My partner Lena drives buses, so between us we're fine, not rich, but we've got about four months saved and we're trying to save for a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: told you so. Everyone at the yard has been going on about AI for two years and my job is still crawling under floors with a torch in my teeth. I'd probably say it at the union meeting too, that we should stop being scared of the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and that's fine. The real worries are the ones I already have: rent going up, Halden taking on cheaper subcontractors, my back at forty. AI was never the thing keeping me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Keep running the crew, keep Dani on track for his licence next year, and keep putting a few hundred a month into the flat fund with Lena. Maybe push the union rep harder on the subcontractor thing, because that's a real threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest. I like being right about stuff like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Halden taking on cheaper subcontractors. How does that touch you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring they brought in a labour-hire outfit for two jobs and the work was rough. I had to go back and fix a board that would've failed inspection. If that keeps happening, that's what squeezes my pay, not a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dani (your apprentice) if he asked whether he picked the right trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dani that people will always need someone they trust in their house with live wires. I'd say a licence on the wall is worth more than any app on your phone. Then I'd make him redo his cable runs, because they're messy.

say: I'd tell the yard **AI was hype** and our trade never needed to worry.
I'd tell the union to focus on the **real threat**, which is cheap subcontractors.
think: Nothing really changes for me, and the worries I have are **rent** and my back.
Labour-hire firms squeezing the **pay rates** scare me more than any computer ever did.
do: Keep running my crew and get **Dani licensed** by next year.
Put a few hundred a month into the **flat fund** with Lena.
Push the union rep on **subcontractor rules** at the next meeting.
feel: **Calm** and a little smug about being right.
Mildly **annoyed** that the old pressures haven't gone away.
S0.quote: A licence on the wall is worth more than any app on your phone.
fieldNote: He defines his worth through his **licence** and his reputation for careful work.
His real threat is **labour-hire firms**, not technology, and he links it straight to the union.
He enjoys being proven right, which hints at how much the AI talk had bothered him.

steps.text: Keep the crew on old-house rewires and get Dani through his licence
Raise subcontractor rules with the union rep at the next branch meeting
Put a few hundred a month into the flat fund with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what matters is who controls it. If the office uses AI to do quotes and scheduling, fine, but it shouldn't be an excuse to cut the two women who run our bookings. I'd say that out loud at the yard and I'd say it at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's closer to me than I like. The robots are slow, so my hands are safe for now. But the office side changes, and I already hate the scheduling app. If they start measuring my crew by what some program thinks a job should take, that's going to be a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every branch meeting and push for an agreement on how AI gets used at Halden: no timing jobs by computer, no cutting office staff without talks. I'd stay on the tools and stay away from the tools on the screen. And I'd keep saving with Lena, but I'd probably hold off on the flat for a year to see how it settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my hands, for everything around them. It's like hearing the neighbours argue through the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay away from the screen tools. What if Halden makes them part of the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'll use what I have to, and nothing more. If they want my crew filling in an AI checklist on a tablet, I'll do it, but I'm not going home to learn it. Bruno (the oldest guy on my crew) says that's how they get you, one form at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra (the office manager at Halden) does quotes, ordering and bookings, which is exactly what the card says goes first. She's been there twenty years and she's the reason my jobs run on time. If Halden (the firm I work for) cuts Sandra (our office manager) to save money, I'd be the first one at the union office.

say: I'd say the question is **who controls** the AI, not whether it arrives.
I'd tell the union nobody in the **office** gets cut without proper talks.
think: My hands are safe for now, but the **office side** of the job is changing fast.
Being timed by a **computer** would start a real fight with management.
do: Push for a **written agreement** at Halden on how AI gets used.
Use only the screen tools I'm **forced** to and nothing more.
Hold off on the **flat** for a year while things settle.
feel: **Uneasy** about everything around his hands, not the hands themselves.
S1.quote: If Halden (the firm I work for) cuts Sandra (our office manager) to save money, I'd be the first one at the union office.
fieldNote: His worry is about **control and fairness**, not his own wage, which still looks safe.
He's protective of office staff he relies on, especially **Sandra**.
He will comply with tools but **refuses to invest** his own time learning them.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a written AI agreement at Halden
Use the tablet checklist only if Halden makes it compulsory
Delay the flat purchase by a year and keep saving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and laws, and we needed them yesterday. I'd be on every post, every meeting, saying the government has to stop the firms rolling robots onto building sites until there are rules. Nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me properly. The office side goes in 2028, so Halden would be run by software, and then by 2031 a robot that can wire a house as well as me? I'd be thirty-two. I don't know how to do anything else and I've never even used one of these AI things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit down with Lena and stop the flat, because I wouldn't sign a mortgage with that coming. I'd build the savings from four months to as much as we can, maybe eight. I'd push the union to fight for licensing, so a qualified person has to sign off every installation even if a robot does the cable runs. I'd vote for whoever promised that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach. Angry too, because it's being done to us, not with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the thinking AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get three years where the office is a computer but my hands still matter. That's the window to get rules in place. If the licensing law isn't written by 2031, a robot will be crawling under that floor instead of me, and I'll be watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena the flat has to wait, and that I'm sorry. Her buses might go driverless before my job goes, honestly, so we'd both be in it. We'd probably just sit there and do the numbers on the back of an envelope.

say: I'd say this is why we need **unions and laws** right now.
I'd call for the government to **pause robots** on building sites until there are rules.
think: By **2031** a robot could wire a house as well as me.
I'd be thirty-two, with **no other skills** and no experience of AI tools.
do: Cancel the **flat purchase** and stretch savings towards eight months.
Push the union to fight for **mandatory sign-off** by licensed electricians.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of losing the only trade he knows.
**Angry** that it's being done to workers, not with them.
S2.quote: If the licensing law isn't written by 2031, a robot will be crawling under that floor instead of me, and I'll be watching it.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as a window to win rules, not to retrain.
Both household incomes feel exposed, since Lena drives **buses**.
He refuses to consider a **new career** even when scared, which ties his fate to politics.

steps.text: Cancel the flat plan and lift savings from four to eight months
Push the union to campaign for licensed sign-off on every installation
Vote for the party that backs electricians' licensing laws

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get this right, so let's not waste them. I'd tell the lads that's long enough for the union to win something real if we all show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years to the AI and eight to the robots means I'm thirty-five when my hands stop being special. That's still young. It's frightening, but it's not a cliff edge tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become a union rep properly, not just turn up to meetings. I'd keep saving, and I think Lena and I would still get a small flat, but a cheaper one, so the mortgage is something one of us could pay alone. I'd keep working like normal because the work's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never learn the AI tools. With five years, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If the union ran a course I'd go. I'd trust the union to teach us what matters, not just sell us something off some ad on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to Lena's family by the sea, which we do every summer. Then eating out. The flat fund is the last thing I'd touch, because that's our future.

say: I'd say five years is long enough for the **union** to win something real.
I'd tell the lads to **show up** and not waste the warning.
think: I'd be **thirty-five** when robots catch up with my hands.
It's frightening, but it's **not a cliff edge** tomorrow.
do: Stand to become a proper **union rep** at Halden.
Buy a **cheaper flat** that one of us could pay for alone.
Join a **union-run course** on AI if one is offered.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier because there's something to do.
S3.quote: I'd trust the union to teach us what matters, not just sell us something off some ad on my phone.
fieldNote: More warning shifts him from anger to **organising**.
He would only learn AI through a source he trusts, which is the **union**.
He plans a **smaller mortgage** so one income could carry it.

steps.text: Stand for the shop steward role at Halden
Buy a smaller flat that one wage could cover
Sign up for a union-run course on AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to sort out rules, and if we don't, it's on us and the politicians. I'd keep saying the same thing about licences and unions, just with less shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years to the AI and thirteen to the robots puts me at forty. That's half a career on the tools, which is more than some trades ever get. I'd probably be fine, and so would most of my crew. It's Dani I'd worry about, because he's only twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. Buy the flat with Lena in a year or two like we planned. Keep up with the union. I'd tell Dani to think about inspection or teaching later on, something that needs a human signature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Knowing robots arrive in thirteen years is like knowing your boiler is old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why worry about Dani (your apprentice) more than yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'll have twenty years in the trade by the time the robots are good. Dani will have barely finished. He'd be starting over at thirty-three with nothing saved, and that's not fair on a kid who did everything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this slower picture that gives you hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to make rules, mostly. If the union and the government do their job, robots could do the boring cable pulling and we'd do the fault finding and sign-off. I could live with that. I just don't believe the firms will share it unless they're made to.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to write proper rules.
I'd keep pushing **licences and unions**, just with less shouting.
think: I'd be about **forty** when robots catch up, half a career in.
My apprentice **Dani** has much more to lose than I do.
do: Buy the **flat** with Lena within two years, as planned.
Tell Dani to aim for **inspection or teaching** work later.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, like an old boiler.
S4.quote: Knowing robots arrive in thirteen years is like knowing your boiler is old.
fieldNote: With a decade's warning his worry moves from himself to his **apprentice**.
He can picture a **fair split** of robot and human work, but doubts firms would share it.
His plans barely change, which fits his **dislike of change**.

steps.text: Buy the flat with Lena within the next two years
Keep attending branch meetings and push for fair robot rules
Carry on running the crew on house rewires

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no contest. Two years for the computer side and five for the robots is nothing, and I'd be thirty-two with no plan. What would help is a strong union with a real seat at the table, and a law that says nobody touches live wiring in a house without a licensed person signing it off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people like me who we trust. I chose this trade because a computer can't crawl under a floor. If that stops being true, I want the union in the room before the robot is. I don't trust the tech firms and I don't fully trust the government either, but I trust the union hall and the guys I work with. If change comes, it has to come through people like that, or nobody will believe it.

headlineQuote: I chose this trade because a computer can't crawl under a floor. If that stops being true, I want the union in the room before the robot is.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old crew lead** who rewires old homes and small shops and never touches AI tools.
He's a committed **union man** who wants change to come through workers, rules and licences, not tech firms.
He shrugs at AI Plateau, grows **uneasy** at Steady Disruption, and is badly shaken by AGI by 2028.
More warning means more **union work** and a smaller flat, not retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because robots would reach his trade around 2031 with no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **strong union** with a real say in how robots come onto sites.
A **licensing law** keeping a qualified person responsible for every live installation.
